challenges.title: A day for one byte
challenges.task: Turn on the human time scale. If reading a register took a third of a second, how long would a core wait for main memory, and for an SSD?
challenges.hint: Read the bars with the human time scale on: every nanosecond becomes a second.
challenges.why: If a register read took a third of a second, main memory would take about a minute and a half and an SSD almost a day. That gap is why processors have caches, and why AI chips put memory as close to the math as they can.

challenges.title: The next memory jump
challenges.task: Bandwidth per GPU grew about 6.6 times from H100 to Rubin. Decide where the next doubling should come from: more stacks, wider stacks or hybrid bonds, and say what your choice assumes.
challenges.hint: Look at what each layer of the package does, then at how bandwidth grew from H100 to Rubin. Which change came from more stacks, and which from wider ones?
challenges.why: There is no single answer. More stacks need a bigger package and more heat removal; wider stacks need finer connections; hybrid bonding needs new factories and good yield on stacked dies. Each bet assumes something different about heat, yield and cost, which is why this is an open problem.

learn.plain: Memory is like a kitchen: a small counter within reach, a fridge across the room, and a shop down the road. Chips keep what they use most on the counter, because every trip further away costs time.
learn.engineer: DRAM retention scales roughly 2× per 10 °C, so refresh (tREFI 3.9 µs, tRFC hundreds of ns) costs a few percent of bandwidth. 3D NAND scales by layer count (286–400+ layers, multi-deck channel-hole etch, CMOS bonded to array) and bits per cell, trading endurance and read margin. HBM4 doubles the interface to 2,048 bits; stack height within 775 µm forces die thinning and pushes hybrid bonding for 16- to 20-high.

quiz.q: Why must DRAM be refreshed constantly?
options: Its tiny capacitors leak charge within milliseconds to seconds
quiz.why: Every row is rewritten at least every 64 ms (32 ms when hot) before the weakest cells fade.

quiz.q: Why do taller HBM stacks push the industry toward hybrid bonding?
options: The stack must fit a fixed height, and removing the bump gap leaves room for thicker, stronger dies
It makes memory faster to manufacture
It removes the need for TSVs
quiz.why: At 16 to 20 dies, micro-bump gaps would force dies thinner than is practical.

options: Stacked DRAM placed beside the processor for very high bandwidth
quiz.why: Rubin carries eight HBM4 stacks for 288 GB of memory.
